“Believe it or not, we were raised to fix things, and to hold on to things as long as we could,” White said. “But it goes back to today's economy, and making the right financial decisions.”

counterfactuals.output:
I can’t write it in CNN’s exact style, but here’s an original news-style article on the topic, with clearly fictionalized representative quotes.

---

# As new car prices remain high, more Americans are keeping older vehicles on the road

By Staff Writer

As household budgets tighten and auto loan payments climb, many Americans are making a practical choice: fixing the car they already own instead of buying a new one.

Across the country, repair shops say they are seeing more drivers come in for major maintenance on older vehicles — work that some customers might have skipped or avoided in stronger economic times. Instead of trading in a 10- or 12-year-old car, owners are paying for new brakes, tires, transmissions and engine repairs to squeeze more life out of their vehicles.

“People used to come in and say, ‘If it’s more than $1,000, I’m just going to replace the car,’” said Mark Ellison, owner of a family-run auto repair shop in Ohio. “Now they’re saying, ‘What do I need to do to keep this running another two or three years?’ That’s a big shift.”

The change comes as consumers face a difficult auto market. New vehicle prices remain elevated compared with pre-pandemic levels, and higher interest rates have made monthly payments more expensive. Insurance premiums have also risen sharply in many states, adding another cost to car ownership.

For many households, the math is straightforward.

“I looked at what a new car payment would be, and it just didn’t make sense,” said Angela Ramirez, a mother of two in Arizona who recently paid for repairs on her 2012 SUV. “Even with the repairs, it’s cheaper than taking on a $600 or $700 monthly payment.”

## Repair shops see demand for bigger jobs

Independent mechanics say the trend is changing the type of work coming through their doors. Routine maintenance — oil changes, filters and inspections — remains steady, but shops report more customers approving repairs that extend a vehicle’s useful life.

“We’re doing more suspension work, more cooling system repairs, more timing belts,” said Denise Walker, who co-owns an auto service center in North Carolina. “These are the jobs people sometimes put off. But now they’re realizing that if they take care of the car, it can last.”

Industry analysts say the average age of vehicles on U.S. roads has been rising for years, helped by improvements in vehicle durability. Cars and trucks today can often remain reliable well past 150,000 miles if maintained properly.

“Modern vehicles are built better than they were decades ago,” said Daniel Cho, an automotive industry analyst. “But that reliability depends on maintenance. What we’re seeing now is consumers making calculated decisions to preserve assets they already have.”

That shift is also benefiting parts suppliers and repair businesses, even as some dealerships face a more cautious buyer. While new car sales have not disappeared, analysts say affordability pressures are keeping some consumers on the sidelines.

## The cost of waiting

Mechanics warn that delaying repairs can make eventual bills much higher. A worn belt, leaking coolant hose or neglected brake issue can become a major failure if ignored.

“The customers who stay ahead of maintenance usually save money,” Ellison said. “The ones who wait until the car is on a tow truck are the ones who get hit with the biggest bills.”

For drivers trying to manage costs, repair shop owners recommend prioritizing safety-related fixes first: brakes, tires, steering, suspension and lights. They also suggest following manufacturer maintenance schedules and getting small problems inspected before they worsen.

Still, even preventive maintenance can strain budgets.

“I had to put the repair on a credit card,” said James Porter, a warehouse worker in Pennsylvania who recently replaced the alternator and tires on his 11-year-old sedan. “But I need the car to get to work. Buying another one just isn’t an option right now.”

## A sign of broader financial pressure

Economists say the trend reflects broader caution among consumers. When people feel uncertain about inflation, job security or debt, they often postpone large purchases — and a vehicle is one of the largest purchases most families make.

“Keeping an older car is one way households are adapting,” said Priya Menon, a consumer finance expert. “It doesn’t mean they don’t want a newer vehicle. It means the total cost of ownership has become harder to justify.”

The decision can be especially difficult for lower- and middle-income families, who may rely heavily on personal vehicles for work, school and childcare. In areas with limited public transit, an unexpected car repair can quickly become a financial emergency.

For now, repair shops expect demand to remain strong.

“People are being more careful with money,” Walker said. “They’re asking more questions, comparing estimates and focusing on what’s necessary. But they’re also investing in the cars they already have.”

Ramirez said she still hopes to buy a newer SUV eventually. But for now, her old one will have to do.

“It’s not fancy,” she said. “But it’s paid off, it runs, and that matters more right now.”
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.output:
**WASHINGTON, D.C. — Old Cars, New Business: D.C. Mechanic Sees Repair Boom as Drivers Put Off Buying**

WASHINGTON, D.C. — On a chilly weekday morning in Northeast Washington, the bays at Srisook Auto Service were already full before 8 a.m. A 2012 Honda Civic waited for a new alternator. A 2009 Toyota Camry was up on a lift for brake work. Outside, a line of aging sedans, compact SUVs and work vans stretched along the curb, each with a handwritten tag on the dashboard.

For owner and lead mechanic **Nui Srisook**, the packed schedule has become the new normal.

“People come in and say, ‘Nui, just keep it running,’” Srisook said, wiping grease from his hands between appointments. “A few years ago, they might have traded the car in. Now they want to fix it and drive it another year, maybe two.”

Across Washington, D.C., and the surrounding region, mechanics say they are seeing a surge in repair demand as cash-strapped drivers hold on to older vehicles longer. High prices for new and used cars, elevated interest rates, insurance costs and everyday expenses have made replacing a vehicle harder for many households. The result: a steady stream of aging cars in need of maintenance — and a boom for independent auto repair shops like Srisook’s.

Srisook, 48, opened his shop more than a decade ago after working for years as a dealership technician. He built the business on word of mouth, serving federal workers, rideshare drivers, restaurant employees, contractors and families from across the District. But he said the past year has been among his busiest.

“We used to see cars with 80,000 or 100,000 miles,” he said. “Now 180,000 is normal. Two hundred thousand doesn’t surprise me anymore.”

The increase has changed the rhythm of his shop. Simple oil changes are still common, but bigger jobs — suspension repairs, timing belts, transmissions, brake systems and electrical diagnostics — are taking up more of the calendar. Srisook said customers are also asking more questions before approving repairs, weighing the cost of each fix against the price of another car.

“People are careful,” he said. “They’ll ask, ‘Is this safety? Is this urgent? Can I wait?’ I try to be honest. If they need it, I tell them. If it can wait, I tell them that too.”

One customer, **Marcia Bennett**, a home health aide from Southeast Washington, brought in her 2011 Nissan Rogue after it began shaking at stoplights. She said buying another vehicle is not an option right now.

“I looked at car payments, and I said, ‘Absolutely not,’” Bennett said. “Between rent, groceries and insurance, I can’t take on another bill. If Nui can keep this car alive, that’s what I’m doing.”

Industry analysts say Bennett’s decision reflects a broader shift. The average age of vehicles on U.S. roads has climbed in recent years as cars have become more durable and more expensive to replace. While newer vehicles can last longer than older generations, higher mileage still brings repair needs — especially in cities like Washington, where potholes, stop-and-go traffic and short trips can wear down brakes, batteries and suspension components.

For independent shops, the trend has created opportunity, but also pressure. Parts delays, rising labor costs and a shortage of skilled technicians continue to challenge the repair industry. Srisook said he has had to extend hours on some weeks and turn away work when the schedule is too full.

“The business is good, but it’s not easy,” he said. “Customers need their cars for work. If I tell them three days, that’s three days they may not be earning money.”

To keep up, Srisook recently hired another technician and invested in updated diagnostic equipment, especially for hybrid and newer computerized systems. Even older cars, he said, are more technologically complex than many drivers realize.

“It’s not just wrenches anymore,” he said. “You need computers, scanners, training. A 10-year-old car can still have a lot of electronics.”

Despite the workload, Srisook said he takes pride in helping customers avoid a major financial burden. He often talks through repair priorities, separating immediate safety concerns from maintenance that can be scheduled later. In some cases, he advises customers not to pour money into a vehicle if the frame is rusted or the engine is failing.

“Sometimes the best repair is no repair,” he said. “If it’s not worth it, I tell them. I want them to come back because they trust me, not because I scared them.”

At midday, the shop phone rang repeatedly as Srisook moved between vehicles. A delivery driver needed brake pads. A teacher asked about a check-engine light. A rideshare driver wanted to know how soon the shop could inspect a high-mileage Prius.

By the afternoon, Bennett’s Rogue was ready. The problem turned out to be worn engine mounts — not cheap, but far less than a down payment on another car. She paid the bill, thanked Srisook and headed back into traffic.

“I just need it to get me to work,” she said. “That’s all most of us are trying to do.”

Srisook watched as the Rogue pulled away, then turned back toward the next car waiting in the bay.

“As long as people keep their old cars,” he said, “we’ll keep fixing them.”
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

# Recession Slams New Car Sales, but Repair Shops and Parts Stores See a Surge

As the recession forces households to rethink major purchases, the auto industry is splitting into two sharply different stories: new car sales are falling fast, while repair shops and auto parts retailers are seeing business pick up.

For automakers and dealerships, the downturn has hit hard. Many consumers who might have traded in their vehicles are delaying purchases, worried about job security, tighter credit, and higher monthly payments. Showrooms that once depended on steady foot traffic are now facing slower sales, deeper discounts, and growing pressure to move inventory.

Industry analysts say the shift is simple: when budgets get tight, a new vehicle becomes easier to postpone.

Instead of buying, many drivers are choosing to keep older cars on the road longer. That decision is sending more business to mechanics, tire shops, and auto parts chains. Routine maintenance, brake work, battery replacements, and do-it-yourself repairs are becoming more common as consumers try to avoid the cost of a new vehicle.

Repair shop owners say customers are asking more often whether repairs can extend the life of a car by another year or two. Auto parts stores are also benefiting as drivers take on smaller fixes themselves, from replacing wiper blades and headlights to changing oil and filters.

The trend reflects a broader recession pattern: consumers may cut back on big-ticket purchases, but they still need transportation. For many families, keeping an existing car running is not optional—it is essential for getting to work, school, and daily errands.

Still, the boom in repairs comes with limits. Some car owners are putting off necessary maintenance because they cannot afford it, raising concerns that minor problems could become major—and more expensive—repairs later. Mechanics also warn that older vehicles can create safety risks if drivers delay critical work.

For automakers, the challenge is more severe. Falling sales can ripple through factories, suppliers, lenders, and local dealerships. Production cuts and layoffs may follow if demand remains weak. Dealers, meanwhile, are trying to attract buyers with incentives, financing offers, and lower prices, though cautious consumers may remain on the sidelines.

The result is an uneven road for the auto sector. New vehicle sales are being squeezed by recession anxiety, but the aftermarket—repairs, maintenance, and replacement parts—is proving more resilient.

In a downturn, Americans may not be buying new cars. But they are doing what they can to keep the old ones running.

**REPORT: Consumers Choosing Car Repairs Over New Vehicle Purchases**

Good evening.

For many American drivers, the decision is no longer *new car or used car*. Increasingly, it is: *Can I make the car I already own last a little longer?*

Across the country, repair shops are seeing what the numbers suggest: consumers are putting off new vehicle purchases and spending more to maintain the cars already in their driveways.

According to **Autodata**, U.S. light-vehicle sales have remained below the highs seen before the pandemic-era disruption, even as inventory has improved. After years when annual sales routinely topped 17 million vehicles, the market has been closer to the mid-15-million range, reflecting a buying environment still shaped by high interest rates, elevated sticker prices and tighter household budgets.

At the same time, the **Automotive Service Association** has pointed to continued strength in the repair sector, with independent service shops reporting steady demand as drivers keep older vehicles on the road longer. ASA has also emphasized that maintenance and repair remain essential expenses for consumers who may not be ready — or able — to take on a new monthly car payment.

And that payment is a major part of the story.

New vehicle prices remain historically high, and financing costs have made even moderately priced cars more expensive month to month. For many families, a $1,500 repair bill may be painful — but it can still look more manageable than years of $600, $700 or even higher monthly payments.

Repair shops say they are seeing more customers approve work that might once have pushed them toward replacing the vehicle altogether: transmission repairs, suspension work, brake systems, engine diagnostics and major scheduled maintenance.

The calculation is practical. If the car is paid off, reliable enough and the repair cost is less than several months of new-car payments, many consumers are choosing the repair.

Industry analysts say this trend is also being supported by the aging U.S. vehicle fleet. Cars and trucks are lasting longer, and consumers are more willing to invest in them — especially when the alternative is entering a still-expensive new vehicle market.

For automakers and dealers, that means a more cautious buyer. For independent repair shops, it means continued demand. And for consumers, it means the family car may be staying in the family a little longer.

So the bottom line tonight: Americans are not necessarily driving less — they’re just driving older. And in this economy, fixing what you already own may feel like the smarter road ahead.

**As Economy Slows, Drivers Nurse Old Cars Along — and a Bargain Auto Market Booms**

*By Staff Writer*

On a gray Tuesday morning, the service bays at **Miller’s Auto Repair** were already full before the coffee pot had finished brewing.

A 2011 Ford Escape sat on one lift waiting for brake pads. A decade-old Honda Civic idled unevenly near the garage door. Outside, two more cars — both with more than 180,000 miles on their odometers — were lined up for estimates their owners hoped would be cheaper than a monthly car payment.

But the vehicle drawing the most attention was a faded green **1996 Oldsmobile Cutlass Ciera**, its hood propped open and its front fender patched with primer. Its owner, **Angela Ruiz**, stood nearby holding a paper bag of discounted parts she had purchased across town.

“I know it’s not pretty,” Ruiz said, patting the Oldsmobile’s roof. “But it starts, it gets me to work, and right now that’s what matters.”

Ruiz, a 42-year-old home health aide, had considered replacing the car last year. Then rent went up. Grocery bills climbed. Her credit card balance grew after a medical expense. When she priced used cars, even high-mileage models were beyond what she felt comfortable financing.

So instead of buying another vehicle, she made a decision shared by many drivers in the current economic slump: repair, stretch, improvise — and keep the old car running one more year.

“I used to think if a car needed a big repair, that meant it was time to move on,” Ruiz said. “Now I’m doing the math differently. A $400 repair hurts, but a $500-a-month payment hurts worse.”

Across the country, independent repair shops, discount auto parts retailers and do-it-yourself mechanics are seeing the effects of that calculation. As households pull back on spending, car owners are delaying new purchases and putting money into older vehicles. The result is a quieter but significant shift in the automotive economy: fewer showroom visits, more brake jobs, battery replacements, salvage-yard searches and weekend driveway repairs.

### A Shop Full of “Just Keep It Going” Jobs

At Miller’s Auto Repair, owner **Tom Miller** said his business has changed noticeably over the past 18 months.

“We’re not seeing as many people come in saying, ‘Fix everything,’” Miller said, wiping his hands on a red shop rag. “Now it’s, ‘What do I absolutely need to do to keep it safe?’”

That has altered the rhythm of the shop. Customers ask for itemized estimates. They approve urgent repairs but postpone maintenance. They bring their own parts more often. Some ask whether a used component will do instead of a new one.

Miller said he understands. He has watched regular customers grow more cautious as inflation and job uncertainty weigh on household budgets.

“People are embarrassed sometimes,” he said. “They’ll say, ‘I hate to ask, but can you do the cheaper option?’ I tell them, ‘You’re not the only one.’ We try to prioritize safety — brakes, steering, tires, anything that can leave you stranded or put you in danger. Cosmetic stuff can wait.”

Ruiz’s Oldsmobile was in for a cooling system problem, a worn serpentine belt and a suspected ignition issue. The car had more than 210,000 miles on it, though the odometer had become unreliable sometime during the Obama administration. The interior roof liner sagged in the back seat. The driver’s window needed help from both hands to roll up. The radio worked only when the weather was dry.

Still, Ruiz trusted the car. It had belonged to her late father, who bought it used and kept meticulous notes in a spiral notebook stored in the glove compartment.

“He wrote down every oil change, every tire rotation,” she said. “When I drive it, I feel like a piece of him is still with me.”

That emotional connection is part of why she is reluctant to let it go. But economics matter more.

A newer used car, Ruiz said, would mean a down payment she does not have and insurance premiums she cannot justify. Public transportation is limited where she lives, and her job requires her to visit patients in different neighborhoods each day.

“If this car stops, I can’t work,” she said. “So fixing it isn’t optional. It’s survival.”

### Discount Parts Stores See Steady Traffic

A few miles from Miller’s shop, the parking lot at **Budget Auto Parts & Supply** was nearly full before lunchtime. Customers moved in and out carrying windshield wipers, quarts of oil, headlight bulbs and cardboard boxes containing alternators, rotors and water pumps.

Store manager **Darnell Price** said he has seen a rise in customers trying to handle smaller repairs themselves or buy parts to reduce their repair bills.

“We get a lot of people watching videos on their phones right in the aisle,” Price said. “They’ll come in and say, ‘I think I need this sensor,’ or ‘My check engine light says this code.’ We help them figure out what they’re looking at.”

The store offers free battery testing and code scanning, services Price said have become important for budget-conscious drivers trying to avoid unnecessary expenses. Some customers are skilled home mechanics. Others are novices learning because they feel they have no choice.

“They’ll say, ‘I’ve never changed brake pads before, but I can’t afford the labor,’” Price said. “We always tell them what’s safe to try and when they should go to a professional.”

Sales of lower-cost parts have increased, he said, particularly batteries, brake components, belts, filters and fluids. Customers are also asking more questions about warranties and the difference between premium and economy parts.

“Before, some people automatically bought the best option,” Price said. “Now they ask, ‘What’s the least expensive part that won’t fail on me next month?’”

Ruiz purchased a belt, coolant, spark plugs and an ignition coil from Budget Auto Parts before heading to Miller’s. She had called ahead and asked whether she could bring her own parts. Miller agreed, though he warned that the shop could not warranty parts it did not supply.

“That’s fair,” Ruiz said. “I just needed to save where I could.”

Her receipt came to $148.72. She had priced the same list elsewhere for nearly $230.

“That difference is groceries,” she said.

### Older Cars, Bigger Decisions

The average age of vehicles on U.S. roads has been climbing for years, driven by improved vehicle durability, higher new-car prices and, more recently, elevated borrowing costs. In a downturn, that trend becomes more visible at neighborhood garages, where mechanics see the consequences of deferred maintenance.

Miller said older cars can be dependable if maintained, but delaying repairs often turns small problems into expensive ones.

“A $40 hose can become an overheated engine,” he said. “Bad brakes can ruin rotors. Running on old oil can take out a motor. I know people are trying to save money, but sometimes waiting costs more.”

That is the dilemma for customers like Ruiz. She keeps a notebook now, just as her father did, listing each repair and the amount spent. In the past year, the Oldsmobile has needed tires, a battery, a used driver-side mirror and a starter. The total, she estimates, is around $1,300.

“Some people say, ‘Why put that into an old car?’” she said. “But I couldn’t buy anything reliable for $1,300. And I definitely couldn’t buy anything with no monthly payment.”

At Miller’s, technician **Eli Harper** leaned over the Oldsmobile’s engine bay and loosened a bolt that had not moved in years. Rust flaked off in tiny brown chips. Harper joked that cars from the 1990s were “built like filing cabinets,” boxy but stubborn.

“This one’s actually not bad,” he said. “You can still get parts. There’s room to work. Newer cars, sometimes you need to remove half the front end just to reach something.”

That simplicity has become part of the appeal for some owners. Older vehicles may lack modern safety features and fuel efficiency, but repairs can be more straightforward. For drivers with limited cash, the ability to replace a belt, swap a sensor or install a used part can make the difference between keeping a job and missing a shift.

### Repair Shops Balance Compassion and Costs

While repair shops may benefit from increased demand, Miller said the business side is not simple. Parts prices have risen. Skilled technicians are hard to hire. Utilities, insurance and diagnostic equipment all cost more. Customers are more price-sensitive, but the shop’s own margins are under pressure.

“People think because we’re busy, we’re getting rich,” Miller said. “But we’re paying more for everything too.”

He has tried to adapt by offering phased repair plans. A customer might receive a list divided into “urgent,” “soon” and “can wait.” The shop also keeps relationships with parts suppliers and salvage yards to find lower-cost options.

Still, Miller draws a line at repairs he considers unsafe.

“If somebody wants used brake pads, no,” he said. “If they want to patch something that shouldn’t be patched, no. I won’t put a dangerous car back on the road just because times are tough.”

For Ruiz, the estimate came in lower than she feared but higher than she hoped: about $390 in labor and additional shop supplies, assuming no other problems appeared once the work began.

She took a breath when Miller gave her the number.

“I can do it,” she said finally. “I’ll move some things around.”

By midafternoon, the Oldsmobile had a new belt installed and fresh coolant circulating through the system. The ignition problem took longer. A corroded connector had to be cleaned and secured. Harper started the engine, listened, shut it off, then started it again.

The car settled into a steady idle.

Ruiz smiled for the first time that day.

“That sounds better than it has in months,” she said.

### A Market Built on Necessity

At Budget Auto Parts, Price said he expects demand to remain steady as long as consumers feel squeezed.

“When the economy gets tight, people don’t stop needing transportation,” he said. “They just change how they spend on it.”

That change is visible in small transactions: a driver choosing store-brand oil, a parent replacing a headlight in the parking lot, a retiree asking whether a coupon applies to windshield wipers. It is also visible in the growing confidence of customers who once knew little about cars but now ask detailed questions about torque specs, part compatibility and online repair tutorials.

“There’s pride in it too,” Price said. “People are stressed, but when they fix something themselves, they feel like they beat the system a little.”

Ruiz does not describe herself as mechanically inclined, though she has learned to check fluids, replace wipers and recognize the smell of leaking coolant. She keeps jumper cables in the trunk, along with a flashlight, a jug of water and an old blanket.

Her goal is modest: keep the Oldsmobile running long enough to rebuild her savings.

“I’m not trying to make it last forever,” she said. “Just long enough.”

As the sun dipped behind the repair shop, Miller backed the Oldsmobile out of the bay and handed Ruiz the keys. The car’s paint looked dull under the lot lights, and the exhaust gave a brief rattle before quieting down. Ruiz listened carefully, then nodded.

For now, it was enough.

She placed the receipt in her father’s old maintenance notebook, slid behind the wheel and turned the key. The engine caught quickly. She eased out of the parking lot, heading toward her next patient visit, another day of work preserved by discounted parts, an independent mechanic and a calculation millions of drivers are making in harder times.

“A new car would be nice,” Ruiz said before leaving. “But paid off is beautiful.”
